short_definition: Loan amortization is the process of paying off a loan through regular scheduled payments, where each payment covers that period's interest first and the remainder reduces the principal balance.
explanation: On a typical amortizing loan, such as many mortgages, car loans and personal loans, the payment stays the same each period but the split inside it changes. Early payments go mostly to interest because the balance is high. Later payments go mostly to principal. An amortization schedule lists this split for every payment.

Understanding amortization shows you the true cost of a loan. A longer term lowers the monthly payment but usually raises the total interest you pay. Extra payments made early can save more interest because they shrink the balance that future interest is charged on.

There are a few things to watch. Some loans charge prepayment penalties. Interest-only or negative-amortization loans can leave the balance flat or even growing. In business accounting, 'amortization' also means spreading the cost of an intangible asset over time, which is a different concept. Always read your loan agreement and check local rules.
example: Illustrative example: A $10,000 loan at 6% annual interest (an illustrative rate) over 12 monthly payments costs about $860.66 a month. In month 1, interest is $50 (0.5% of $10,000), so $810.66 reduces the balance to $9,189.34. In month 2, interest falls to about $45.95, so more of the payment goes to principal. Total interest over the year comes to about $328.
common_mistake: Choosing the longest loan term because the monthly payment looks small, without checking how much extra total interest it adds over the life of the loan.
title: Loan Amortization
